kernelIdea: x² ≥ 0 for every real x, so x² + 1 = 0 has no real solution. Roots of polynomials matter enough that mathematicians extended the number system rather than accept the gap.

kernels.l1: Counting numbers tell you how many. They do not turn you around — so people made a new number whose whole job is turning.
kernels.l2: Every square you can build holds a real, countable amount — never less than nothing. So no number, multiplied by itself, points you backwards, and that gap is what a new number was built to fill.
kernels.l3: No number on the number line, multiplied by itself, gives a negative answer. So x × x = −1 has no answer among the numbers we have, and mathematicians built a new number to answer it.
kernels.l4: Multiplying any real number by itself gives an answer that is zero or bigger, so nothing on the number line squares to −1. Rather than accept that gap, mathematicians built a larger number system — exactly as they once did to make subtraction and then division always work.
kernels.l5: Multiplying a real by itself never gives a negative, so nothing on the number line squares to −1. The discriminant in the quadratic formula is where this gap shows up in practice.
kernels.l6: The reals fall short in the simplest possible case: nothing squares to −1. Extending the number system is the standard response to a failure like that.
kernels.l7: Since every real square is non-negative, nothing on the number line squares to −1. Extending the number system rather than accepting the gap is the same move that produced the integers, the fractions and the reals.
kernels.l8: No real number squares to −1, so that equation has no real solution. Adding one solution turns out to supply solutions for every equation built from powers of x at once.

kernel: x² ≥ 0 for every real x, so x² + 1 = 0 has no real solution and the polynomial x² + 1 has no real root. Roots of polynomials matter enough that mathematicians extended the number system rather than accept the gap.
objectives: Explain why x² + 1 has no real root
